responses.tip: Estimate first.
Took 4 from 6 in the tenths. Ask: is 8.25 more than 8.4 − 0.5?

strings.title: Split a Factor
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Split one factor into friendly parts (like 10 and 2), multiply each part, then add the products.
strings.keywords: split, partial products, distributive property, ten and some more
strings.connection: Builds on facts to 10 × 10. Facts to 12 × 12 come from a ten fact plus a small fact.
watchFor: Splitting both factors and multiplying only matching parts (12 × 7 as 10 × 7 + 2 = 72): ask "Did every part of 12 get multiplied by 7?"
Adding instead of multiplying a part (12 × 7 = 70 + 2 + 7): draw the area model and ask "What is the area of the small piece?"
Skip counting from 0 every time: accept it, then ask "Is there a fact you already know that's close?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 10 × and 2 × help you with 12 ×?" Land: split a factor into friendly parts, multiply each part, and add. The area model shows every piece.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: array 7 x 10
Look for: a double. Ask: "Hold on to this one too." Model: array 7 x 2
Look for: 10 × 7 + 2 × 7 = 70 + 14. Ask: "How did the first two help?" Word choice: "I split 12 into 10 and 2." Model: area 10+2 x 7

responses.say: 10 sevens is 70 and 2 sevens is 14, so 84.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: where are the 70 and the 14?

responses.say: I see it in the dots: a 10 part and a 2 part.

responses.tip: Using a known fact. Accept it.
Only multiplied the 10. Ask: did every part of 12 get multiplied by 7?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 8 + 2 × 8 = 80 + 16. Ask: "Can you split it the same way?" Model: area 10+2 x 8

responses.tip: Doubling. Name it: × 8 is double, double, double.
Ask: what is 2 × 8? Where is that piece in the area model?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 9 + 1 × 9 = 90 + 9. Ask: "What friendly split works here?" Model: area 10+1 x 9

responses.tip: Over and back. We'll do more on Day 3.
Ask: is 11 × 9 the same as 10 × 10? Draw both.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 12 + 2 × 12 = 120 + 24. Ask: "Which factor did you split?" Model: area 10+2 x 12

responses.tip: Four parts. Ask: why are there four pieces?
Missed two pieces. Draw the area model and ask: what is in the other two boxes?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 15 + 2 × 15 = 150 + 30. Ask: "Does splitting still work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 10+2 x 15

responses.tip: Split the other factor. Both work.
A Day 4 strategy. Accept and name it.

strings.title: Area Model with Two Splits
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Split both factors by place value, find the four partial products, and add them.
strings.keywords: area model, partial products, tens and ones, place value
strings.connection: Day 1 split one factor. Today both factors are split by place value, so the area model has four parts.
watchFor: Multiplying only tens by tens and ones by ones (14 × 15 = 100 + 20 = 120): ask "How many boxes are in the area model? Did you fill them all?"
Place-value slips in a partial product (10 × 20 = 20): ask "Is that ten twenties?"
Losing track of the partial products: write each one inside its box, then add.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How does the area model show every partial product?" Land: split both factors by place value; there is a product for every box, and the boxes add to the answer.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick ten fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 10 x 10+5

responses.tip: Ask: why does × 10 make the digits shift?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 × 10 + 4 × 5, or double 15 twice. Ask: "What do you know about 15s?" Model: area 4 x 10+5
Look for: 150 + 60. Ask: "How do the last two help?" Word choice: "14 fifteens is 10 fifteens and 4 fifteens." Model: area 10+4 x 10+5

responses.tip: Uses the helper problems. Ask: where are they?
The target model. Ask: what's in each box?
Missed two boxes. Ask: how many boxes are in the area model?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 10 + 60 + 3. Ask: "What are the four boxes?" Model: area 10+3 x 20+1

responses.tip: Split only one factor. Good choice here.
Ask: how many 13s are you adding? 20 or 21?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 40 + 40 + 8. Ask: "Is there a way with fewer boxes?" Model: area 20+4 x 10+2

responses.tip: Connect: the algorithm's rows are partial products too.
Missed a box. Ask: show me all four boxes.

problems.notes: Look for: 600 + 90 + 40 + 6. Ask: "Which box is the biggest? About how big is the answer?" Model: area 30+2 x 20+3

responses.tip: Ask: where is 96 in the area model? (the 3 row: 90 + 6)
Missed two boxes. Ask: did every part of 32 get multiplied by every part of 23?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 80 + 50 + 20, or 25 × 4 = 100 thinking. Ask: "Which way is quickest?" Model: area 20+5 x 10+4

responses.tip: Uses 4 quarters make a dollar. Name it.

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: When a factor is close to a friendly number, multiply by the friendly number, then take away the extra group.
strings.keywords: friendly number, over, take back, one group too many
strings.connection: Like Week 1 Day 2 (add a friendly number, then adjust), but with groups: going over by 1 means one whole group too many.
watchFor: Taking back 1 instead of one group (19 × 15 = 300 − 1 = 299): ask "How many 15s did you add too many? How much is that?"
Taking back from the wrong factor (19 × 15 = 300 − 19): draw the area model and ask "What is the size of the strip you're taking away?"
Adding the extra group instead of subtracting: ask "Did you make too many groups or too few?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we take away 15 and not 1?" Land: 20 × 15 is one group of 15 too many, so take away a whole group.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 15 = 30, so 20 × 15 = 300. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 20 x 10+5
Look for: 300 − 15. Ask: "How is 19 × 15 different from 20 × 15?" Word choice: "19 fifteens is one fifteen less than 20 fifteens." Model: area 20-1 x 15

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: what's in the strip we took away?
Splitting works too. Ask: which is quicker?
Took away 1, not one group. Ask: how many 15s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 24 = 48, then × 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: ratio 1:24, 2:48, 20:480
Look for: 480 − 24. Ask: "How much do you take away this time?" Model: area 20-1 x 24

responses.tip: Shows the subtraction. Good.
Took away a 19. Ask: what is the size of the strip, 19 or 24?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 × 12 = 360, then − 12. Ask: "What's the friendly number?" Model: area 30-1 x 12

responses.tip: Added instead of taking away. Ask: is 29 more or less than 30?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 × 15 = 450, then + 15. Ask: "Over or under this time?" Model: area 30+1 x 15

responses.tip: Under, then add a group. Ask: why add?
Took away when 31 is more than 30. Ask: too many groups or too few?

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 25 = 500, then − 2 × 25 = 50. Ask: "How many groups too many?" Model: area 20-2 x 25

responses.tip: Tomorrow's strategy. Name it.
Ask: 2 what? How big is each group?

strings.title: Double and Halve
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Halve one factor and double the other; the product stays the same, and the new problem can be easier.
strings.keywords: double, halve, same area, rearrange, friendly factor
strings.connection: Days 1 to 3 split a factor. Today we change both factors without changing the product.
watchFor: Doubling (or halving) both factors (16 × 15 → 32 × 30): cut the rectangle and ask "Did the area stay the same?"
Halving an odd number and getting stuck: ask "Which factor is easier to halve?"
Not seeing when to use it: ask "Which factor would you like to turn into 10, 50 or 100?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does the product stay the same?" Land: cut the rectangle in half and put the halves together; the area doesn't change. Halve the even factor, double the other, and look for 10s and 100s.

problems.notes: Look for: 8 × 3 = 24, then × 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 8 x 30
Look for: halve 16, double 15 → 8 × 30. Ask: "Why is it the same answer as the last one?" Word choice: "I halved 16 and doubled 15." Model: halve 16 x 15 = 8 x 30

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why is the area the same?
Doubled both. Ask: is 32 × 30 the same area? Draw both rectangles.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 × 50. Ask: "Which factor would you like to double?" Model: halve 14 x 25 = 7 x 50
Look for: 9 × 10. Ask: "What happens when you double 5?" Model: halve 18 x 5 = 9 x 10
Look for: 6 × 70. Ask: "Halve which one?" Model: halve 12 x 35 = 6 x 70

responses.tip: Halved only one. Ask: what did you do to the other factor?

problems.notes: Look for: 12 × 50, then 6 × 100. Ask: "Can you do it again?" Model: halve 24 x 25 = 12 x 50 = 6 x 100

responses.tip: Twice. Ask: why stop at 6 × 100?

problems.notes: Look for: double 15, halve 18 → 30 × 9. Ask: "Which factor do you halve this time?" Model: halve 15 x 18 = 30 x 9

responses.tip: Over and back. Good.

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Look at the numbers first, then choose: split a factor, go over and back, or double and halve.
strings.keywords: choose, efficient, friendly numbers, split, over and back, double and halve
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4.
watchFor: Using the same strategy for every problem: ask "What do you notice about these numbers before you start?"
Forgetting to adjust after going over: ask "How many groups too many?"
Not checking reasonableness: ask "About how big should the answer be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which strategy did you choose for each problem, and what about the numbers made you choose it?" Land: numbers near a ten → over and back; an even factor and a 5 or 25 → double and halve; otherwise split by place value.

problems.notes: Look for: double and halve to 100 × 4. Ask: "What do you notice about 25?" Model: halve 25 x 16 = 50 x 8 = 100 x 4

responses.say: 4 quarters in a dollar, 16 is 4 fours: 400.

problems.notes: Look for: 230 + 23. Ask: "What's friendly about 11?" Model: area 10+1 x 23

responses.tip: Ask: how many 23s? Show the extra strip.

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 12 − 12. Ask: "Which number is close to a friendly number?" Model: area 20-1 x 12

responses.tip: Ask: one what? How big is the group?

problems.notes: Look for: 7 × 70. Ask: "Is there an even factor to halve?" Model: halve 14 x 35 = 7 x 70
Look for: 20 × 13 + 13. Ask: "Have we seen these numbers before?" (13 × 21 on Day 2). Model: area 20+1 x 13

responses.say: It's the same as 13 × 21 from Tuesday.
responses.tip: Commutative property. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 50 × 12 − 12. Ask: "What's the friendly number?" Model: area 50-1 x 12

responses.tip: Ask: how many 12s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 18 × 50, 9 × 100. Ask: "How many times can you halve 36?" Model: halve 36 x 25 = 18 x 50 = 9 x 100

strings.title: Multiplying by Tenths
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To multiply a whole number by decimal tenths, find one tenth first (× 0.1), then build up the tenths you need: 0.3 is 3 tenths, 1.5 is one whole and 5 tenths.
strings.keywords: one tenth, times 0.1, tenths, build up, ratio table, half
watchFor: Thinking × 0.5 makes the number bigger: ask "What is half of 120?"
120 × 0.3 = 3.6 (multiplying 12 × 3 and placing the decimal by habit): ask "About how much should it be? Is it close to a third of 120?"
Forgetting the whole part in 450 × 1.1: ask "What's 450 × 1? And then the 0.1 part?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the first problem help with all the others?" Land: one tenth of the number is the building block. Multiply it to get any number of tenths, and add the whole number when there's a whole part.

problems.notes: Look for: one tenth of 120. Ask: "What does × 0.1 do?" Word choice: "one tenth of 120". Model: ratio 1:120, 0.1:12

responses.tip: Hold on to this. It's the building block.
Multiplied by 10. Ask: is 0.1 more or less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 tenths is 5 × 12, or half of 120. Ask: "What fraction is 0.5?" Model: ratio 1:120, 0.1:12, 0.5:60

responses.say: 0.5 is a half, so half of 120 is 60.
One tenth is 12, five tenths is 60.
responses.tip: Built up from 0.1.
Ask: should 120 × 0.5 be more or less than 120?

problems.notes: Look for: 120 + 60. Ask: "How does 120 × 0.5 help?" Model: ratio 1:120, 0.5:60, 1.5:180

responses.tip: The whole part plus the tenths.
Forgot the whole part. Ask: is 1.5 more or less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: a tenth of 240 is 24, three tenths is 72. Ask: "What's one tenth of 240?" Model: ratio 1:240, 0.1:24, 0.3:72

responses.say: A tenth is 24, three tenths is 72.

responses.tip: Split the whole number.
Ask: is 7.2 close to a third of 240?

problems.notes: Look for: a tenth is 35, two tenths is 70. Ask: "Could you also think of it as a fifth?" Model: ratio 1:350, 0.1:35, 0.2:70

responses.say: A tenth of 350 is 35, double it is 70.
0.2 is one fifth, and a fifth of 350 is 70.
responses.tip: Fraction connection.

problems.notes: Look for: 450 + 45. Ask: "What's the whole part? What's the tenth?" Model: ratio 1:450, 0.1:45, 1.1:495

responses.tip: Added 1 instead of one tenth of 450. Ask: what is 450 × 0.1?

strings.title: Dividing Decimals by Whole Numbers
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Divide a decimal by a whole number by thinking in tenths or hundredths (2.4 is 24 tenths), or by splitting it into friendly parts to share.
strings.keywords: share, divide, tenths, hundredths, friendly parts, estimate
watchFor: Putting the decimal in the wrong place (2.4 ÷ 4 = 6): ask "Is 6 more or less than 2.4? Can sharing make it bigger?"
Dividing only the whole part (7.5 ÷ 5 = 1.5 fine, but 3.6 ÷ 4 = 0.9 written as 0.09): ask "How many tenths is 3.6?"
Not estimating first: ask "About how much should each share be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How does thinking in tenths help?" Land: 3.6 is 36 tenths, and 36 tenths ÷ 4 is 9 tenths. Estimate first so the decimal point lands in a sensible place.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 2.4. Ask: "What's half of 2? Half of 0.4?" Word choice: "2.4 shared into 2". Model: area 2.4 / 2 = 2 + 0.4

responses.say: Half of 2 is 1, half of 0.4 is 0.2. 1.2.

responses.tip: Thinking in tenths.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 1.2, or 24 tenths ÷ 4 = 6 tenths. Ask: "Is the answer more or less than 1?" Model: text 2.4 = 24 tenths ; 24 tenths ÷ 4 = 6 tenths ; = 0.6

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Used the last problem: halve again.
Ask: can 4 people sharing $2.40 each get $6?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 ÷ 3 and 0.6 ÷ 3. Ask: "Which parts are easy to share by 3?" Model: area 3.6 / 3 = 3 + 0.6
Look for: 36 tenths ÷ 4 = 9 tenths. Ask: "Why can't we split it into 3 and 0.6 this time?" Model: ratio 4:3.6, 1:0.9

responses.tip: Ask: is 4 × 0.09 close to 3.6?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 ÷ 5 and 2.5 ÷ 5. Ask: "What's a friendly part of 7.5?" Model: area 7.5 / 5 = 5 + 2.5

responses.tip: Ask: about how much is 7.5 ÷ 5? Is 15 sensible?

problems.notes: Look for: 48 tenths ÷ 6 = 8 tenths. Ask: "Is the answer more or less than 1? How do you know?" Model: ratio 6:4.8, 1:0.8
Look for: 0.8 ÷ 4 and 0.04 ÷ 4, or 84 hundredths ÷ 4. Ask: "What changes with hundredths?" Model: area 0.84 / 4 = 0.8 + 0.04

responses.tip: Ask: can sharing 0.84 give each person more than 0.84?

strings.title: Dividing by Tenths
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing by a decimal tenth asks how many of those tenths fit: 12 ÷ 0.1 is 120 because 10 tenths fit in each whole. Then group the tenths: 12 ÷ 0.4 is 120 tenths in groups of 4.
strings.keywords: how many fit, tenths, groups of, ten times as many, ratio table
watchFor: Expecting division to make smaller (12 ÷ 0.1 = 1.2): ask "How many tenths fit in one whole? In 12?"
Stopping at the tenths count (12 ÷ 0.4 = 120): ask "How many tenths are in each 0.4?"
Losing a zero with 240 ÷ 0.3: ask "About how many 0.3s fit in 240? More or less than 240?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does dividing by a tenth make the answer bigger?" Land: lots of small pieces fit. Count the tenths (× 10), then group them by the numerator. A ratio table keeps the count straight.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 tenths in each whole. Ask: "How many tenths fit in 1? In 12?" Word choice: "how many tenths fit in 12". Model: ratio wholes:tenths, 1:10, 12:120

responses.tip: Hold on to this.
Found a tenth of 12. Ask: how many tenths fit in 12?

problems.notes: Look for: 120 tenths in groups of 2. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: ratio count:amount, 1:0.2, 5:1, 60:12

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Five 0.2s fit in each whole.
Ask: is 2.4 groups of 0.2 equal to 12?

problems.notes: Look for: half of the last answer. Ask: "Bigger pieces, so more or fewer fit?" Model: ratio count:amount, 1:0.4, 5:2, 30:12

responses.say: 0.4 is double 0.2, so half as many: 30.
responses.tip: Used the last one.
Counted tenths. Ask: how many tenths are in each 0.4?

problems.notes: Look for: 360 tenths ÷ 4. Ask: "What changed from 12 ÷ 0.4?" Model: ratio count:amount, 30:12, 90:36

responses.tip: Scaled the last row.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 halves per whole. Ask: "What fraction is 0.5?" Model: ratio count:amount, 1:0.5, 2:1, 90:45

responses.tip: 0.5 is a half.
Found half of 45. Ask: how many halves fit in 45?

problems.notes: Look for: 2400 tenths ÷ 3. Ask: "About how big should it be?" Model: ratio count:amount, 1:0.3, 10:3, 800:240

responses.say: 10 jumps of 0.3 is 3, and 240 is 80 threes: 800.

responses.tip: Ask: is 80 × 0.3 equal to 240?

strings.title: Thousandths Make a Whole
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Add and subtract decimals to thousandths by jumping to a whole number first, or by changing a number to a friendlier one and adjusting.
strings.keywords: thousandths, whole number, make a whole, give and take, compensate, friendly number
watchFor: Lining up digits from the right (0.125 + 0.9 = 0.134): ask "About how much should it be?"
Treating 0.875 + 0.125 as 0.1000: ask "How many thousandths make a whole?"
Forgetting to adjust after rounding 1.999 to 2: ask "Where did the 0.001 go?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which numbers made you think of jumping to a whole?" Land: look for pieces that make a whole (0.125 and 0.875, 0.75 and 0.25). Estimate first so the answer is sensible.

problems.notes: Look for: 125 + 875 thousandths is 1000 thousandths. Ask: "How many thousandths make a whole?" Word choice: say "one hundred twenty-five thousandths". Model: numberline 0.125 +0.875

responses.tip: Fraction connection.
Ask: is the answer more or less than 0.875?

problems.notes: Look for: the same pair, 2 more wholes. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 2.125 +0.875

responses.say: Same as the last one, plus 2: 3.

problems.notes: Look for: 0.875 to make 3, then 0.025 more. Ask: "How much more is 0.9 than 0.875?" Model: numberline 2.125 +0.875 +0.025

responses.tip: Make a whole.
Over and back.
Lined up from the right. Ask: is 0.9 nine tenths or nine thousandths?

problems.notes: Look for: back 0.4 to 3, then up 0.275; or back 0.1 then 0.025. Ask: "What's a friendly place to land?" Model: numberline 3.4 -0.1 -0.025

responses.tip: Writing the zeros helps the algorithm.
Lined up from the right. Ask: is 3.321 about 3.4 take away an eighth?

problems.notes: Look for: up from 2.75 to 3 (0.25), then to 6 (3). Ask: "How far apart are they?" Model: numberline 2.75 >3 >6

responses.tip: Adding up.
Over and back.

problems.notes: Look for: 1.999 is 0.001 from 2. Ask: "What's 1.999 close to?" Model: givetake 1.999 + 2.345 = 2 + 2.344

responses.tip: Give and take.
Forgot to adjust. Ask: where did the 0.001 go?

strings.title: Whole Numbers Times Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To multiply a whole number by a fraction, find one part first (divide by the denominator), then take as many parts as the numerator says.
strings.keywords: of, unit fraction, one part, numerator, denominator, bar model
watchFor: Multiplying the whole number by the denominator (12 × 3/4 = 48/4 and stopping): ask "Is 3/4 of 12 more or less than 12?"
Dividing by the numerator instead of the denominator: ask "How many equal parts is the bar split into?"
Thinking the answer should be bigger than the whole number: ask "What is 1/2 of 20?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 1/4 of 20 help with 3/4 of 20?" Land: find one part by dividing by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 12 × 3/4 and 3/4 of 12 are the same.

problems.notes: Look for: 20 split into 4 equal parts. Ask: "How big is one part?" Word choice: "one fourth of". Model: bar 1/4 of 20

responses.tip: One part first.

responses.say: Half of 20 is 10, half of that is 5.

problems.notes: Look for: three of those parts. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: bar 3/4 of 20

responses.say: One fourth is 5, so three fourths is 15.
responses.tip: The target strategy.
Whole minus one part. Clever.
Ask: is three quarters of 20 more or less than 20?

problems.notes: Look for: one fifth is 6, two fifths is 12. Ask: "What's one part?" Model: bar 2/5 of 30

responses.say: A fifth of 30 is 6, two fifths is 12.

responses.tip: Divided by the numerator. Ask: how many equal parts does the bar have?

problems.notes: Look for: the same as 3/4 of 12. Ask: "Is 12 × 3/4 the same as 3/4 of 12?" Model: bar 3/4 of 12

responses.say: 3/4 of 12: one fourth is 3, three fourths is 9.
responses.tip: Ask: why can we switch it to 3/4 of 12?
Multiply first, then divide. Same answer.
Forgot the fourths. Ask: should 12 × 3/4 be bigger than 12?

problems.notes: Look for: a third of 15 is 5, two thirds is 10. Ask: "Which is easier: divide first, or multiply first?" Model: bar 2/3 of 15

responses.say: A third of 15 is 5, two thirds is 10.

problems.notes: Look for: an eighth of 24 is 3, five eighths is 15. Ask: "What's one eighth?" Model: bar 5/8 of 24

responses.say: An eighth of 24 is 3, so 5 eighths is 15.
Half of 24 is 12, plus one more eighth (3) is 15.
responses.tip: 5/8 as a half and an eighth.
Divided by the numerator. Ask: what does the 8 tell us?

problems.notes: Look for: an eighth of 40 is 5, three eighths is 15. Ask: "What do you notice about the last two answers?" Model: bar 3/8 of 40

responses.say: An eighth of 40 is 5, three eighths is 15.

strings.title: Dividing Whole Numbers by Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing a whole number by a fraction asks how many of those fractions fit. Count how many unit fractions fit, then group them: 4 ÷ 2/3 is 12 thirds in groups of 2, which is 6.
strings.keywords: how many fit, unit fraction, groups of, number line, measure
watchFor: Expecting the answer to be smaller than the whole number: ask "How many halves fit in 2?"
Stopping at the unit fraction count (4 ÷ 2/3 = 12): ask "How many thirds are in one 2/3?"
Multiplying instead (6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2): ask "Are we finding a part of 6, or how many 3/4s fit?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 4 ÷ 1/3 help with 4 ÷ 2/3?" Land: count how many unit fractions fit (multiply by the denominator), then put them into groups (divide by the numerator).

problems.notes: Look for: 2 halves in each whole. Ask: "How many halves fit in 2?" Word choice: "how many 1/2s fit in 2". Model: numberline 0 +1/2x4

responses.tip: Found half of 2. Ask: how many halves fit in 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 thirds per whole, 4 wholes. Ask: "Hold on to this one." Model: numberline 0 +1/3x12

responses.tip: Hold on to this.

problems.notes: Look for: 12 thirds in groups of 2. Ask: "How does 4 ÷ 1/3 help?" Model: numberline 0 +2/3x6

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Counted thirds, not two-thirds. Ask: how many thirds in one 2/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 24 fourths in groups of 3. Ask: "How many fourths in 6?" Model: numberline 0 +3/4x8

responses.tip: Multiplied. Ask: are we finding 3/4 of 6, or how many 3/4s fit?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 fifths in groups of 3. Ask: "What's the same as the last one?" Model: numberline 0 +3/5x5
Context: "5 m of ribbon, cut into 1/2 m pieces." Look for: 2 pieces per metre. Ask: "How many pieces?" Model: numberline 0 +1/2x10

responses.tip: Ask: can cutting 5 m into half-metres give only 2 1/2 pieces?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 fifths in groups of 2 is 7 groups, with 1 fifth left (half a group). Ask: "What do we do with the leftover fifth?" Model: numberline 0 +2/5x7 +1/5

responses.say: 7 jumps of 2/5 is 2 4/5, and the last 1/5 is half a jump: 7 1/2.
responses.tip: Ask: why half a jump?
Named the leftover in fifths. Ask: what part of a 2/5 jump is 1/5?

strings.title: Fifths and Tenths
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Halves, fifths and tenths all fit together because tenths are the common piece: 1/2 = 5/10 and 1/5 = 2/10.
strings.keywords: common denominator, equivalent fractions, tenths, fifths, halves, rename
watchFor: Adding tops and bottoms (1/2 + 3/10 = 4/12): ask "Is 4/12 more than 1/2?"
Renaming 2/5 as 2/10: ask "How many tenths are in one fifth?"
Forgetting to simplify 8/10: ask "Can you name 8/10 with fifths?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why are tenths so useful here?" Land: a half is 5 tenths and a fifth is 2 tenths, so tenths are a common piece. Rename, then add or subtract the tenths.

problems.notes: Look for: 5/10 + 3/10 = 8/10 = 4/5. Ask: "How many tenths is a half?" Word choice: "same-sized pieces". Model: numberline 0 +1/2 +3/10

responses.tip: Ask: why does 8/10 equal 4/5?
Decimals are tenths too.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 4/12 more than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 4/10 + 3/10. Ask: "How many tenths in 2/5?" Model: numberline 0 +2/5 +3/10

responses.tip: Renamed 2/5 as 2/10. Ask: how many tenths in one fifth?

problems.notes: Look for: 6/10 + 5/10 = 11/10. Ask: "Is it more than 1?" Model: numberline 3/5 +2/5 +1/10

responses.tip: Make a whole.

problems.notes: Look for: 10/10 − 3/10. Ask: "How many tenths in 1?" Model: numberline 1 -3/10
Look for: 8/10 − 5/10. Ask: "How does the first problem help?" Model: numberline 1/2 >4/5

responses.say: From 1/2 up to 4/5 is 3/10, just like the first problem.

responses.tip: Subtracted tops and bottoms. Ask: is the answer really 1?

problems.notes: Look for: back 2/10 to 2, then 5/10 more to 1 1/2. Ask: "Can you go through the whole number?" Model: numberline 2 1/5 -1/5 -1/2

strings.title: One Percent and Five Percent
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: 1% is one hundredth of the number. Build other percents from it: 5% is 5 × 1% (or half of 10%), 6% is 5% + 1%, 99% is 100% − 1%.
strings.keywords: percent, one hundredth, 1%, 5%, 10%, build up, take away
watchFor: Finding 1% by dividing by 10: ask "Is 1% one tenth or one hundredth?"
Thinking 99% must be hard: ask "How far is 99% from 100%?"
Losing the decimal with 1% of 450: ask "About how much is one hundredth of 450?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 1% help with every other percent?" Land: 1% is the number ÷ 100. Then build: 5% is five of them or half of 10%, and 99% is the whole take away 1%.

problems.notes: Look for: 300 ÷ 100. Ask: "What is one hundredth of 300?" Word choice: "percent means out of 100". Model: ratio 100:300, 1:3

responses.tip: That's 10%. Ask: is 1% one tenth or one hundredth?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 × 3, or half of 10% (30). Ask: "How does 1% help?" Model: ratio 100:300, 1:3, 5:15

responses.tip: Half of 10%. Also great.

problems.notes: Look for: 5% + 1% = 15 + 3. Ask: "Which two percents add to 6%?" Model: ratio 100:300, 1:3, 5:15, 6:18

responses.tip: Adding percents.

problems.notes: Look for: 100% − 1% = 300 − 3. Ask: "How far is 99% from 100%?" Model: ratio 100:300, 1:3, 99:297

responses.tip: Take away from the whole.
Ask: is 99% almost all of 300, or a tiny bit?

problems.notes: Look for: 450 ÷ 100. Ask: "Where does the decimal go?" Model: ratio 100:450, 1:4.5

responses.tip: That's 10%. Ask: what's one hundredth of 450?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 10% (45), or 5 × 4.5. Ask: "Which way is easier here?" Model: ratio 100:450, 10:45, 5:22.5
Look for: 4 × 4.5, or 5% − 1%. Ask: "Could you take away instead?" Model: ratio 100:450, 1:4.5, 4:18

strings.title: Unit Rates
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Find the unit rate first (how much for 1), then scale it to any amount. On a double number line, both lines grow at the same rate.
strings.keywords: rate, unit rate, per, for each, double number line, scale
watchFor: Adding instead of scaling (4 km in 20 min, so 10 km in 26 min): ask "Is the walker going the same speed?"
Dividing the wrong way (4 ÷ 20): ask "How many minutes for 1 km?"
Not using rows they have: ask "Which mark on the line is closest?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did the unit rate help so much?" Land: once you know the minutes for 1 km, any distance is just that many groups. Both lines on the double number line grow by the same factor.

problems.notes: Context: "A walker goes 4 km in 20 minutes." Look for: ÷ 4 both. Ask: "How long for 1 km?" Word choice: "5 minutes per kilometre". Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 4:20, 1:5

responses.tip: The unit rate.
That's km per minute. Ask: what are we asked: minutes for 1 km?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 5. Ask: "How does the unit rate help?" Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 1:5, 4:20, 10:50

responses.tip: Added 6 to both. Ask: is the walker going the same speed?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 × 5, or 4 km + 2 km. Ask: "Could you use 4 km?" Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 2:10, 4:20, 6:30

responses.say: 4 km is 20 min, 2 km is 10 min: 30.
responses.tip: Adding parts.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 km take away 1 km. Ask: "Which mark is closest?" Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 1:5, 9:45, 10:50
Look for: 60 minutes ÷ 5. Ask: "How far in an hour?" Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 4:20, 12:60

responses.say: Three times 20 minutes, so three times 4 km: 12.
responses.tip: Scaling by 3.
Using the unit rate backward.
Found how many 20-minute blocks. Ask: how many km in each block?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 km + 5 km = 50 + 25. Ask: "Which two marks add to 15?" Model: doubleline km:min, 0:0, 5:25, 10:50, 15:75

strings.title: Which Is the Better Buy?
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To compare two prices, find the unit price (the cost of 1) for each, or scale both to the same number of items.
strings.keywords: unit price, rate, per, better buy, compare, same number of items
watchFor: Comparing the totals ($6 vs $8.40) without the number of cans: ask "Do they give you the same number of cans?"
Dividing the wrong way (cans per dollar vs dollars per can): ask "What does 1.5 mean here?"
Thinking the bigger pack is always cheaper: ask "Is it, per can?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you decide which was the better buy?" Land: compare the same number of items: the unit price (cost of 1), or the cost of the same amount, like 12 cans each.

problems.notes: Context: "Store A: 4 cans for $6." Look for: $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50. Ask: "How much for one can?" Word choice: "unit price", "per can". Model: ratio cans:dollars, 4:6, 1:1.5

responses.tip: The unit price.

responses.say: Half of 6 is 3 for 2 cans, half again is 1.50.
responses.tip: Halving twice.
That's cans per dollar. Ask: what does the question ask: dollars for one can?

problems.notes: Context: "Store B: 6 cans for $8.40." Look for: $8.40 ÷ 6 = $1.40. Ask: "Which store is cheaper per can?" Model: ratio cans:dollars, 6:8.4, 1:1.4

responses.say: $8.40 ÷ 6 is $1.40, so Store B is cheaper.
Store A, because $6 is less than $8.40.
responses.tip: Compared totals. Ask: do they give the same number of cans?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 times Store A's deal. Ask: "What's 12 cans at Store A?" Model: ratio cans:dollars, 4:6, 12:18
Look for: double Store B's deal. Ask: "Does it agree with the unit prices?" Model: ratio cans:dollars, 6:8.4, 12:16.8

responses.tip: Same number of cans: easy to compare.
Added 6 to both. Ask: does 12 cans cost only $6 more than 6 cans?

problems.notes: Context: "Store C: 5 cans for $7." Look for: $7 ÷ 5 = $1.40. Ask: "How does C compare with B?" Model: ratio cans:dollars, 5:7, 1:1.4

responses.say: $1.40 a can, the same as Store B.

problems.notes: Look for: 6 packs of 5. Ask: "What would 30 cans cost at each store?" Model: ratio cans:dollars, 5:7, 30:42

responses.tip: Using the unit price.

strings.title: 50% and 25%: Halve It
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 50% is half, and 25% is half of a half, so find them by halving.
strings.keywords: percent, per hundred, half, quarter, halve, benchmark
strings.connection: Connects percents to fractions students already know: 50% = 1/2 and 25% = 1/4.
watchFor: Dividing by the percent (25% of 80 = 80 ÷ 25 = 3.2): ask "Should 25% of 80 be more or less than half of 80?"
Subtracting the percent (25% of 80 = 55): ask "Is 25% a part of the 80 or an amount to take away?"
Thinking 75% needs a new start: ask "How many 25%s make 75%?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 50% help with 25%?" Land: 100% is the whole, 50% is half, 25% is half of that. Halving is a fast way to find these percents.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 80. Ask: "What does 50% mean?" Word choice: "50 out of every 100, so half." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 50:40, 100:80

responses.say: 50% is half, and half of 80 is 40.
responses.tip: The target model. Ask: where is 100%?
Divided by the percent. Ask: should 50% of 80 be bigger or smaller than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 40. Ask: "How does 50% help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:20, 50:40, 100:80

responses.say: Half of 80 is 40, half of 40 is 20.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why halve twice?

responses.say: Like 4 quarters in a dollar: 80 split into 4.

responses.tip: Divided by the percent. Ask: is 25% of 80 more or less than half of 80?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 36. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 50:18, 100:36

responses.say: Half of 30 is 15, half of 6 is 3: 18.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 18. Ask: "How did the last one help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:9, 50:18, 100:36

responses.tip: Subtracted. Ask: is 25% an amount to take away, or a part of 36?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 140 is 70, half of 70 is 35. Ask: "Halve, then halve again?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:35, 50:70, 100:140

responses.tip: Split the whole. Good thinking.
Subtracted. Ask: should 25% of 140 be more or less than half of 140?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 9, or 36 − 9. Ask: "How many 25%s make 75%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:9, 50:18, 75:27, 100:36

responses.tip: Take away a quarter. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 45. Ask: "What is half of 45?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:22.5, 50:45, 100:90

responses.tip: Ask: can we share the 2 that's left? What's half of 1?

strings.title: 10% and 1%
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 10% is one tenth (divide by 10) and 1% is one hundredth (divide by 100).
strings.keywords: percent, tenth, hundredth, divide by 10, divide by 100, place value
strings.connection: Day 1 halved. Today we divide by 10 and 100 and see the digits shift.
watchFor: Mixing up 10% and 1% (10% of 350 = 3.5): ask "Is 10% a tenth or a hundredth?"
Dropping a zero that isn't there (10% of 64 = 6): ask "What is 64 ÷ 10? What happens to the 4?"
Thinking 1% is always 1: ask "Is 1% of 400 the same as 1% of 4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How are 10% and 1% related?" Land: 10% is one tenth (÷ 10), and 1% is a tenth of that (÷ 100). Then build other percents from them.

problems.notes: Look for: 400 ÷ 10. Ask: "What does 10% mean?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40
Look for: 40 ÷ 10, or 400 ÷ 100. Ask: "How does 10% help?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40, 1:4

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why ÷ 10 again?
Ask: is 1% of 400 the same as 1% of 100?

problems.notes: Look for: 350 ÷ 10. Ask: "What happens to the digits?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 10:35

responses.tip: Found 1%. Ask: is 10% a tenth or a hundredth?

problems.notes: Look for: 35 ÷ 10. Ask: "Can you divide 35 by 10?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 10:35, 1:3.5

responses.say: 10% is 35, a tenth of that is 3.5.

responses.tip: Stopped at 10%. Ask: is 1% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 64 ÷ 10 = 6.4. Ask: "What happens to the 4?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:64, 10:6.4

responses.tip: Dropped the 4. Ask: what is 4 ÷ 10?

problems.notes: Look for: 1% is 3.5, double it. Ask: "Which percent from today helps?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 1:3.5, 2:7

responses.say: 10% is 35, 2% is a fifth of that: 7.

problems.notes: Look for: 10% + 1% = 40 + 4. Ask: "Can you build 11% from today's percents?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40, 1:4, 11:44

responses.tip: Ask: should 11% of 400 be more or less than 400?

strings.title: 5% and 15%
strings.label: Day 3
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 5% is half of 10%, and 15% is 10% + 5%.
strings.keywords: percent, half of 10%, build up, combine, tip
strings.connection: Combines Day 1 (halving) and Day 2 (10%). Useful for tips and taxes.
watchFor: Dividing by 5 for 5% (5% of 60 = 12): ask "Is 5% more or less than 10%?"
Adding the percent to the number (15% of 80 = 95): ask "Is 15% a part of 80 or extra?"
Losing track when building 15%: write each part on the double number line.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 10% help with 5% and 15%?" Land: find 10%, halve it for 5%, then add them for 15%.

problems.notes: Look for: 60 ÷ 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:6, 100:60
Look for: half of 10%. Ask: "How does 10% help?" Word choice: "5% is half of 10%." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 10:6, 100:60

responses.say: 10% is 6, so 5% is half of that: 3.
responses.tip: The target strategy.
Divided by 5. Ask: is 5% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 + 3. Ask: "Can you build 15% from the last two?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 10:6, 15:9, 100:60

responses.tip: Added the percent. Ask: should 15% of 60 be more or less than 60?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 8, 5% = 4, 15% = 12. Ask: "Same steps?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:4, 10:8, 15:12, 100:80

responses.say: 10% is 8, and 15% is one and a half times that.

responses.tip: Ask: is 15% a part of 80 or extra?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 24, half is 12. Ask: "What's 10% first?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:12, 10:24, 100:240

responses.tip: Divided by 5. That's 20%. Ask: is 5% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 24 + 12. Ask: "How did the last one help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:12, 10:24, 15:36, 100:240
Look for: 3 + 1.5. Ask: "What would a 15% tip on $30 be?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:1.5, 10:3, 15:4.5, 100:30

responses.tip: Ask: should a 15% tip be more or less than the meal?

strings.title: Build from 10% and 25%
strings.label: Day 4
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: Use a benchmark percent you know (10% or 25%) and multiply or combine it to get the percent you need.
strings.keywords: benchmark, build up, multiply, 20%, 30%, 75%, 90%
strings.connection: Days 1 to 3 found single benchmarks. Today we scale them: 30% is 3 × 10%, 75% is 3 × 25%.
watchFor: Dividing by the percent (20% of 70 = 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5): ask "Should 20% be more or less than 10%?"
Not seeing 90% as 100% − 10%: ask "Is 90% close to a percent you know?"
Losing the whole: keep 100% labeled on the double number line.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which benchmark did you start from for each one?" Land: start from 10% or 25%, then multiply, add, or subtract from 100%.

problems.notes: Look for: 70 ÷ 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 100:70
Look for: 2 × 7. Ask: "How many 10%s in 20%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 20:14, 100:70

responses.tip: The target strategy.
A fraction connection. Name it.
Divided by the percent. Ask: should 20% be more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 7. Ask: "Can you keep going?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 20:14, 30:21, 100:70

responses.tip: Subtracted the percent. Ask: is 30% a part of 70?

problems.notes: Look for: half of half of 120. Ask: "Which benchmark is this?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:30, 50:60, 100:120
Look for: 3 × 30, or 120 − 30. Ask: "How did the last problem help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:30, 50:60, 75:90, 100:120

responses.tip: Subtracted the percent. Ask: is 75% more or less than half?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 4.5, × 4 = 18; or 20% = 9, × 2. Ask: "Which benchmark is easiest here?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:4.5, 20:9, 40:18, 100:45

responses.tip: Building down. Nice.

problems.notes: Look for: 100% − 10% = 70 − 7. Ask: "Is 90% close to a percent you know?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 90:63, 100:70

responses.tip: Ask: what does 90% of something mean? Is it most of it?

strings.title: Choosing a Percent Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: Look at the percent and the number, then choose: halve, divide by 10 or 100, or build from benchmarks.
strings.keywords: benchmark, choose, combine, 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4.
watchFor: Using only one benchmark for everything: ask "Is there a quicker benchmark for this one?"
Not checking reasonableness: ask "Is the answer more or less than half? Should it be?"
Missing that a% of b = b% of a (60% of 25 = 25% of 60): ask "What if we switch the numbers?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which benchmark did you use for each, and why?" Land: find a benchmark (50%, 25%, 10%, 5%, 1%) and build from it. Check that the answer makes sense.

problems.notes: Look for: 25% + 10% = 20 + 8, or 3 × 10% + 5%. Ask: "Which benchmarks make 35%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:8, 25:20, 35:28, 100:80

responses.tip: Ask: should 35% of 80 be more or less than half of 80?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% + 2 × 1% = 20 + 4. Ask: "Can 1% help?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:200, 10:20, 1:2, 12:24
Look for: 50% − 5% = 30 − 3. Ask: "Is 45% close to a benchmark?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 45:27, 50:30, 100:60

responses.tip: Building down from 50%.
Ask: should 45% of 60 be close to half of 60?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 2.5, × 6; or 25% of 60 = 15. Ask: "What if you switch the numbers?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:2.5, 20:5, 60:15, 100:25

responses.say: It's the same as 25% of 60, a quarter of 60: 15.
responses.tip: Great noticing. Ask: why does switching work?

problems.notes: Look for: 25% + 1% = 12.5 + 0.5. Ask: "Which benchmark is close to 26%?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:50, 25:12.5, 1:0.5, 26:13

responses.say: 50 is half of 100, so 26% of 50 is half of 26.
responses.tip: Great connection to "per hundred".
Ask: should 26% of 50 be more or less than half of 50?

problems.notes: Look for: 100% − 1% = 300 − 3. Ask: "Is 99% close to a percent you know?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:300, 1:3, 99:297
Look for: 3 × 12, or 48 − 12. Ask: "Which benchmark do you start from?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:12, 75:36, 100:48

strings.title: Halves, Quarters and Thirds on the Clock
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Think of fractions as parts of an hour: change each fraction to minutes, add the minutes, then change back.
strings.keywords: fraction of an hour, minutes, common unit, unlike denominators
strings.connection: Students know 1/2 hour = 30 min and 1/4 hour = 15 min. Minutes are a common unit, so unlike denominators can be added.
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6): ask "Is 2/6 more or less than 1/2? Can the sum be smaller than one of the parts?"
Mixing up minutes and the fraction (35 minutes = 35/100): ask "How many minutes in a whole hour?"
Answers over 1 written as improper only: accept, then ask "How many whole hours is that?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did minutes make these easy?" Land: minutes are a common unit (sixtieths). To add unlike fractions, change them to the same unit first.

problems.notes: Look for: 30 + 15 = 45 minutes, 3/4 of an hour. Ask: "How many minutes is each?" Model: clock 1/2 + 1/4

responses.say: 30 minutes and 15 minutes is 45 minutes, that's 3/4.
responses.tip: The target model.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 2/6 more or less than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. Ask: "What fraction of an hour is 35 minutes?" Word choice: "35 out of 60 minutes, that's 7/12." Model: clock 1/4 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: how do you know 35 minutes is 7/12?
Twelfths: 5-minute chunks. Connect.
Ask: is 2/7 more or less than 1/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 + 20 = 50 minutes. Ask: "How far from a whole hour?" Model: clock 1/2 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/5 more or less than 1/2?

strings.title: Sixths and Twelfths
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Sixths are 10 minutes and twelfths are 5 minutes; use minutes (or twelfths) as the common unit.
strings.keywords: sixths, twelfths, fifths, minutes, common denominator, equivalent fractions
strings.connection: Day 1 used halves, quarters and thirds. Today: smaller parts. Notice that twelfths are 5-minute chunks, so they work like a common denominator.
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/6 + 1/3 = 2/9): ask "Is 2/9 more or less than 1/3?"
Not simplifying (30/60, 6/12) and thinking it's a different number: ask "Is 30 minutes the same as half an hour?"
Wrong minutes for a sixth (1/6 = 6 minutes): ask "How many sixths in an hour? So how many minutes each?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How are minutes like a common denominator?" Land: change each fraction to the same unit (minutes, sixtieths, or twelfths), add, then simplify.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 + 20 = 30 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is a sixth?" Model: clock 1/6 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/9 more or less than 1/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 + 15 = 25 minutes. Ask: "What fraction is 25 minutes?" Model: clock 1/6 + 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/10 more or less than 1/4?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 + 5 = 55 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is a twelfth?" Model: clock 5/6 + 1/12

responses.tip: Ask: is 6/18 more or less than 5/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 25 + 20 = 45 minutes. Ask: "Where have we seen 45 minutes?" Model: clock 5/12 + 1/3

responses.tip: Correct! Ask: is there a simpler name for 9/12?

responses.tip: Ask: 5/6 is almost an hour. Can adding 1/4 give less than 1?
