strings.title: Comparing Mixtures
strings.label: Day 13
strings.group: Grade 8 · Unit · Rates and Proportional Reasoning
strings.strategy: To compare two mixtures, make one part the same in both, or find what percent of each mixture is concentrate. Then the comparison is fair.
strings.keywords: concentrate, mixture, stronger, part to part, part to whole, percent, compare
watchFor: Comparing the differences (Mix B has 2 more cups of water than concentrate, Mix A only 1): ask "Does the difference tell you how strong it tastes?"
Mixing part-to-part and part-to-whole: ask "Is 2 out of 3, or 2 out of 5 cups?"
Thinking more concentrate always means stronger: ask "What about the water?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which mix is stronger, and how do you know?" Land: compare fairly by making the concentrate the same (6 cups in each) or by finding the percent of concentrate in the whole mixture.

problems.notes: Context: "Mix A: 2 cups orange concentrate for 3 cups water. Mix B: 3 cups concentrate for 5 cups water." Look for: ×3. Ask: "How much water with 6 cups of concentrate in Mix A?" Word choice: "concentrate", "stronger". Model: ratio concentrate:water, 2:3, 6:9
Look for: ×2. Ask: "Now compare: which has more water for the same concentrate?" Model: ratio concentrate:water, 3:5, 6:10

responses.say: Double Mix B: 6 concentrate, 10 water. B is weaker.
responses.tip: Same concentrate, more water: weaker.

responses.say: B is stronger, because it has 3 cups of concentrate.
responses.tip: Ask: B has more water too. Is it a fair comparison?

problems.notes: Look for: Mix A is 2 cups concentrate out of 5 cups total. Ask: "What percent of Mix A is concentrate?" Model: ratio concentrate:total, 2:5, 40:100

responses.tip: Part to whole.
Used part to part (2 to 3). Ask: how many cups are in the whole mix?

problems.notes: Look for: Mix B is 3 out of 8 cups. Ask: "What's 1 out of 8 as a percent?" Model: ratio concentrate:total, 1:8, 3:24, 37.5:100
Context: "Mix C: 5 cups concentrate for 7 cups water." Look for: ×3. Ask: "Compare C with A: 15 concentrate each?" Model: ratio concentrate:water, 5:7, 15:21

responses.say: 15 concentrate needs 21 water in Mix C.
Mix A with 15 concentrate would be 22.5 water, so C is stronger.
responses.tip: Ask: why does less water mean stronger?

problems.notes: Context: "Mix D: 1 cup concentrate for 3 cups water." Look for: 1 out of 4 cups total. Ask: "Part to whole: 1 out of how many?" Model: ratio concentrate:total, 1:4, 25:100

responses.say: 1 out of 4 cups is 25%, the weakest.

responses.tip: Part to part again. Ask: how many cups in the whole mix?

strings.connection: Day 8: Percent as a Rate per 100

strings.title: Rates with Parts of an Hour
strings.label: Day 14
strings.group: Grade 8 · Unit · Rates and Proportional Reasoning
strings.strategy: When a rate is given for part of an hour (2 km in half an hour), scale up to 1 hour to get the speed, then use it for other times.
strings.keywords: speed, km per hour, part of an hour, half, quarter, scale up
watchFor: Treating the given distance as the hourly speed (2 km in 1/2 h = 2 km/h): ask "How far in a whole hour?"
Dividing instead of multiplying (2 ÷ 2 = 1): ask "Is a whole hour longer or shorter than half an hour?"
Stuck with 15 minutes: ask "How many quarter hours in an hour?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you get to a whole hour each time?" Land: if you know a part of an hour, multiply up: ×2 for a half, ×4 for a quarter, ×(4/3) for three quarters. That's the speed per hour.

problems.notes: Context: "A hiker walks 2 km in half an hour." Look for: double. Ask: "How far in a whole hour?" Word choice: "km per hour". Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.5:2, 1:4

responses.tip: Ask: is a whole hour longer or shorter than half an hour?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 h = 8 km, half hour = 2 km. Ask: "How does 4 km/h help?" Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.5:2, 2:8, 2.5:10
Context: "A cyclist goes 1.5 km in 15 minutes." Look for: ×4. Ask: "How many quarter hours in an hour?" Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.25:1.5, 1:6

responses.tip: Added. Ask: what does 0.25 mean here?

problems.notes: Look for: three quarter hours: 3 × 1.5. Ask: "Is it more or less than 6?" Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.25:1.5, 0.75:4.5, 1:6

responses.tip: From the whole hour.

problems.notes: Context: "A runner covers 3 km in 45 minutes." Look for: 1 km per 15 min, so 4 km per hour. Ask: "What's 15 minutes?" Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.25:1, 0.75:3, 1:4

responses.say: 15 min is 1 km, so an hour is 4 km.
responses.tip: Through a quarter hour.
Multiplied. Ask: in a whole hour, more or less than 3 km?

problems.notes: Context: "A swimmer swims 6 km in 1.5 hours." Look for: ÷3. Ask: "How many half hours in 1.5 hours?" Model: doubleline hours:km, 0:0, 0.5:2, 1.5:6

strings.connection: Day 5: Speed on a Double Number Line

strings.title: Tax and Tip
strings.label: Day 15
strings.group: Grade 8 · Unit · Rates and Proportional Reasoning
strings.strategy: Sales tax and tips are percents of a price. Find a friendly percent (10%, 1%, 5%) and build the rest. The total is the price plus the percent, or 113% of the price.
strings.keywords: percent, tax, HST, tip, 13%, 15%, total, build up
watchFor: Adding 13 dollars instead of 13% (40 + 13 = 53): ask "Is the tax 13 dollars or 13 percent?"
Finding only the tax when the total is asked: ask "What will you actually pay?"
Stuck on 13%: ask "What are 10%, 1% and 3%?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you build 13% and 15%?" Land: 13% is 10% + 3 × 1%; 15% is 10% + half of 10%. The total is 100% + the percent: 113% or 115% of the price.

problems.notes: Context: "Ontario HST is 13%. A game costs $40." Look for: 10% is 4, 1% is 0.4, so 4 + 1.2. Ask: "How much tax?" Word choice: "13% of the price". Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:40, 10:4, 1:0.4, 3:1.2, 13:5.2

responses.tip: Building 13%.
Ask: is it 13 dollars or 13 percent?

problems.notes: Look for: 40 + 5.20. Ask: "What will you pay at the till?" Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:40, 13:5.2, 113:45.2

responses.tip: The multiplier from Grade 7.

problems.notes: Look for: double the last tax. Ask: "How does 13% of 40 help?" Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:80, 10:8, 3:2.4, 13:10.4

responses.tip: Twice the price, twice the tax.

problems.notes: Context: "A 15% tip on a $60 meal." Look for: 10% is 6, 5% is 3. Ask: "What's half of 10%?" Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:60, 10:6, 5:3, 15:9

responses.tip: Ask: is it $15 or 15%?

problems.notes: Look for: 60 + 9. Ask: "What's the total with tip?" Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:60, 15:9, 115:69

responses.tip: Found only the tip. Ask: what will you actually pay?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 2.5, 3% = 0.75. Ask: "What's 1% of 25?" Model: ratio percent:dollars, 100:25, 10:2.5, 3:0.75, 13:3.25

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 16
strings.group: Grade 8 · Unit · Rates and Proportional Reasoning
strings.strategy: Look at the numbers first, then choose: a friendly row, the unit rate, the multiplier across, or a percent. Explain why it fits.
strings.keywords: choose, unit rate, across, ratio table, double number line, percent, explain
watchFor: Using the same strategy for every problem: ask "What do you notice about these numbers?"
Adding instead of multiplying: ask "Is the rate the same in every row?"
Not checking the answer makes sense: ask "About how big should it be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which strategy did you choose for each, and why?" Land: friendly factors suggest building rows; awkward factors suggest the unit rate or the multiplier across; 'out of' suggests scaling to 100.

problems.notes: Look for: ×4 down. Ask: "What do you notice about 3 and 12?" Model: ratio 3:8, 12:32

responses.tip: A friendly factor down.

problems.notes: Look for: ÷15 to 3:4, then 75:100. Ask: "Out of 100?" Model: ratio part:whole, 45:60, 3:4, 75:100

responses.tip: Added 40. Ask: is it still 45 out of 60?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 25 + 0.2 × 25. Ask: "Which kind of problem is this?" Model: ratio cm:km, 1:25, 3:75, 0.2:5, 3.2:80
Look for: 5.6 ÷ 4, halve twice: 2.8, 1.4. Ask: "Unit rate?" Model: ratio items:dollars, 4:5.6, 2:2.8, 1:1.4

responses.tip: Divided the wrong way. Ask: dollars for one item?

problems.notes: Look for: ×5. Ask: "What's the whole if 20% is 9?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 20:9, 100:45
Look for: no friendly factor: across ×3/7, or the unit rate 3/7. Ask: "Is the answer a whole number? How do you know?" Model: text unit rate: 3/7 ; 10 x 3/7 = 30/7 = 4 2/7

responses.tip: When nothing is friendly, the unit rate always works.
Added 3. Ask: does the second number stay less than half the first?

strings.connection: Days 1 to 15

strings.title: Groups of Negatives
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 8 · Week 3 · Multiplying and Dividing Integers
strings.strategy: A positive times a negative is that many groups of the negative, so the product is negative.
strings.keywords: groups of, repeated addition, jumps left, negative product
strings.connection: First string of the week. Builds on adding integers (Grade 7): 4 × −3 is −3 + −3 + −3 + −3.
watchFor: Making the product positive (4 × −3 = 12): ask "Four groups of −3: are we gaining or owing?"
Adding instead of multiplying (4 × −3 = 1): ask "What does 4 × mean?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 4 × −3 negative?" Land: 4 × −3 is four jumps of −3 (four groups of debt), so the product is negative.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 0 +3x4
Look for: four groups of −3. Ask: "What changed from the last one?" Word choice: "Four groups of negative three." Model: numberline 0 -3x4

responses.tip: The target model.

responses.say: Four groups of three red tiles: 12 negatives.

responses.tip: Ask: four groups of −3: where do you end up, left or right of 0?

problems.notes: Look for: two jumps of −5. Ask: "Positive or negative? How do you know before calculating?" Model: numberline 0 -5x2
Look for: 6 × 4 = 24, negative. Ask: "Do you need to draw it?" Model: numberline 0 -4x6

responses.say: 6 × 4 is 24, and it's groups of a negative: −24.

responses.tip: Added. Ask: is that 6 groups of −4?

problems.notes: Look for: ten groups of −7. Ask: "How does × 10 work with negatives?" Model: text 10 x -7 = -70

responses.tip: Ask: ten groups of a debt of 7: do you owe or have?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 10 × −12. Ask: "Which strategy from multiplying whole numbers helps?" Model: text 10 x -12 = -120 ; 5 x -12 = -60

responses.tip: × 5 as half of × 10. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 25 × 4 = 100 (quarters), negative. Ask: "What do you know about 25 × 4?" Model: text 25 x 4 = 100 ; 25 x -4 = -100

responses.say: 4 quarters is a dollar, so 25 × 4 = 100. Negative: −100.

responses.tip: Added instead of multiplying. Ask: is that 25 groups of −4?

strings.title: Taking Away Groups
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 8 · Week 3 · Multiplying and Dividing Integers
strings.strategy: A negative times a number means taking away that many groups; add zero pairs first so there is something to take away.
strings.keywords: take away groups, zero pairs, opposite, negative times negative
strings.connection: Day 1 was groups of negatives. Today the first factor is negative: take away groups, using zero pairs from Grade 7.
watchFor: Thinking −3 × −2 is negative ("negatives make it negative"): build it with tiles and ask "What is left after we take away three groups of −2?"
Forgetting to add zero pairs: ask "There's nothing on the mat. How can we take away?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does taking away negatives leave positives?" Land: −3 × −2 means take away three groups of −2; after adding zero pairs and removing the negatives, six positives are left.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: tiles 3 x 2
Look for: take away three groups of 2. Ask: "What could −3 groups mean?" Word choice: "Take away three groups of 2." Model: tiles -3 x 2

responses.say: Add 6 zero pairs, take away three groups of 2 positives: 6 negatives left.
responses.tip: The target model. Ask: why add zero pairs?

problems.notes: Look for: take away three groups of −2. Ask: "What's left this time?" Model: tiles -3 x -2

responses.say: Add 6 zero pairs, take away three groups of −2: 6 positives left.
It's the opposite of 3 × −2, which is −6.
responses.tip: The opposite of the opposite. Name it.
Ask: after taking away the negatives, which tiles are left?

problems.notes: Look for: the opposite of 4 × −5. Ask: "Can you predict the sign first?" Model: tiles -4 x -5

responses.say: Take away four groups of −5: 20 positives left.

responses.tip: Ask: what's the opposite of 4 × −5?

problems.notes: Look for: take away two groups of 7. Ask: "Positive or negative?" Model: tiles -2 x 7
Look for: opposite of 6 × −6. Ask: "Do you need the tiles now?" Model: text 6 x -6 = -36 ; -6 x -6 = 36

responses.tip: Ask: taking away groups of negatives leaves what?

problems.notes: Look for: opposite of 10 × −9. Ask: "What's the sign rule you're noticing?" Model: text 10 x -9 = -90 ; -10 x -9 = 90

strings.title: The Pattern of Products
strings.label: Day 3
strings.group: Grade 8 · Week 3 · Multiplying and Dividing Integers
strings.strategy: Following a pattern: as one factor goes down by 1, the product changes by the other factor, even past zero.
strings.keywords: pattern, decrease by, sign, continue the pattern
strings.connection: Days 1 and 2 built the sign rules with models. Today a pattern shows why −1 × −4 must be 4.
watchFor: Stopping at 0 × −4: ask "What comes next in the pattern?"
Continuing the pattern the wrong way (−1 × −4 = −4): ask "What has been happening to the product each time?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the pattern show −1 × −4 = 4?" Land: each step down in the first factor adds 4 to the product, so after 0 the products become positive.

problems.notes: Look for: three groups of −4. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 0 -4x3
Look for: −8. Ask: "How did the product change?" Model: text 3 x -4 = -12 ; 2 x -4 = -8

responses.tip: Ask: why up by 4?

problems.notes: Look for: up by 4 again. Ask: "What's the pattern?" Model: text 3 x -4 = -12 ; 2 x -4 = -8 ; 1 x -4 = -4

responses.say: −4. Each time the product goes up 4.

problems.notes: Look for: zero groups is 0, and it fits the pattern. Ask: "Does the pattern agree?" Model: text 1 x -4 = -4 ; 0 x -4 = 0

responses.say: Zero groups of anything is 0. And −4 + 4 = 0.

problems.notes: Look for: continue the pattern: up 4 again. Ask: "What must come next?" Word choice: "The pattern says it goes up by 4 each time." Model: text 0 x -4 = 0 ; -1 x -4 = 4

responses.say: The product keeps going up by 4: 4.
responses.tip: The target reasoning.

responses.say: Take away one group of −4: 4 positives left.
responses.tip: Connects to Taking Away Groups.
Ask: what's been happening to the product each step?

problems.notes: Look for: 8. Ask: "Does the pattern keep going?" Model: text -1 x -4 = 4 ; -2 x -4 = 8
Look for: jump ahead in the pattern. Ask: "Can you skip to it?" Model: text -5 x -4 = 20

responses.tip: Ask: what does the pattern say happens past 0?

strings.title: Dividing Integers
strings.label: Day 4
strings.group: Grade 8 · Week 3 · Multiplying and Dividing Integers
strings.strategy: Use the related multiplication fact: −12 ÷ 3 = −4 because 3 × −4 = −12; the sign follows the same rules.
strings.keywords: related facts, fact family, inverse, quotient, sign
strings.connection: Uses Days 1 to 3: every division has a related multiplication, so the same sign rules apply.
watchFor: Getting the size right but the sign wrong: ask "What times 3 makes −12?"
Reversing dividend and divisor: ask "Which number is being shared or grouped?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did multiplication help you divide?" Land: every division has a related multiplication; the same sign rules apply: same signs give a positive, different signs a negative.

problems.notes: Look for: three groups of −4. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 0 -4x3
Look for: 3 × −4 = −12, so −4. Ask: "How does the last problem help?" Word choice: "−12 shared into 3 equal groups." Model: numberline 0 -4x3

responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: Split −12 into 3 equal jumps: each is −4.

responses.tip: Ask: 3 times 4 is 12, not −12. What times 3 is −12?

problems.notes: Look for: how many groups of −4 in −12? Ask: "Same fact family?" Model: numberline 0 -4x3

responses.tip: Ask: −4 × −3 is what? Is it −12?

problems.notes: Look for: −5 × −4 = 20. Ask: "What times −5 gives 20?" Model: text -5 x -4 = 20 ; 20 / -5 = -4

responses.tip: Ask: −5 × 4 is what?

problems.notes: Look for: −9 × 4 = −36. Ask: "Positive or negative? Why?" Model: text -9 x 4 = -36 ; -36 / -9 = 4

responses.tip: Ask: −9 × −4 is what?

problems.notes: Look for: 25 × −4 = −100. Ask: "Which fact do you know?" Model: text 25 x -4 = -100 ; -100 / 25 = -4
Look for: 7 × 12 = 84, same signs. Ask: "How do you know the sign first?" Model: text -7 x 12 = -84 ; -84 / -7 = 12

responses.tip: Split the dividend. Nice.

strings.title: Choosing an Integer Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.group: Grade 8 · Week 3 · Multiplying and Dividing Integers
strings.strategy: Decide the sign first (count the negatives), then find the size with a friendly strategy.
strings.keywords: sign first, count the negatives, size, related fact, friendly numbers
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4, and extends to three factors: an even number of negatives makes a positive product.
watchFor: Getting the size right but the sign wrong: ask "Before you calculate, positive or negative? How do you know?"
Thinking two negatives always make a positive, even when adding (−3 + −4 = 7): ask "Are we adding or multiplying?"
Three factors: losing track of the sign. Ask "How many negative factors are there?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How can you know the sign before you calculate?" Land: count the negative factors: an even number gives a positive, an odd number a negative. Then find the size with any friendly strategy.

problems.notes: Look for: sign first (one negative: negative), then 6 × 4. Ask: "Positive or negative? How do you know?" Model: text 6 x 4 = 24 ; -6 x 4 = -24

responses.say: 6 × 4 is 24, and one negative makes it negative: −24.
responses.tip: Sign first, then size.

responses.say: Take away 6 groups of 4: 24 negatives left.

responses.tip: Ask: how many negative factors? So positive or negative?

problems.notes: Look for: the related fact from the last problem. Ask: "How does −6 × 4 help?" Model: text -6 x 4 = -24 ; -24 / -6 = 4

responses.tip: Ask: −6 × −4 is what? Is it −24?

problems.notes: Look for: two negatives: positive; 5 × 8 = 40. Ask: "Do you need a model, or do you know the sign?" Model: text 5 x 8 = 40 ; -5 x -8 = 40

responses.say: Two negatives make a positive product: 40.
Take away 5 groups of −8: 40 positives left.
responses.tip: Day 2's model.
Ask: what's the opposite of 5 × −8?

problems.notes: Look for: count the negatives (two: positive), then 3 × 4 × 5. Ask: "How many negative factors?" Model: text 3 x -4 = -12 ; -12 x -5 = 60

responses.tip: Step by step.

responses.say: Two negatives, so positive. 4 × 5 is 20, times 3 is 60.
responses.type: two negatives: positive ; 3 x 4 x 5 = 3 x 20 = 60
responses.tip: Sign first, friendly order. Name it.
Ask: how many negative factors are there? Even or odd?

problems.notes: Look for: 8 × −9 = −72. Ask: "What times 8 gives −72?" Model: text 8 x -9 = -72 ; -72 / 8 = -9

responses.tip: Split −72 into 8 equal jumps of −9.
Ask: 8 × 9 is 72, not −72. What times 8 is −72?

problems.notes: Look for: three negatives: odd, so negative. Ask: "Even or odd number of negatives?" Model: text -2 x -3 = 6 ; 6 x -5 = -30

responses.say: Three negatives is odd, so negative: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30, so −30.

responses.tip: Ask: how many negatives? Do they all pair up?

problems.notes: Look for: same signs: positive; 12 × 12 = 144. Ask: "Which fact do you know?" Model: text 12 x 12 = 144 ; -144 / -12 = 12

responses.tip: Ask: −12 × −12 is what?

strings.title: Adding Near a Ten

problems.notes: Look for: 38 + 100, then back 2. Ask: "How is this like problems 3 to 6? What changed?" Word choice: go over the ten (or hundred), then take back the extra.

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why back 2?
Took back 1. Ask: how far is 98 from 100?

strings.title: Give and Take
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Move an amount from one number to the other so the total stays the same and one number becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: give, take, move, same total, balance.
strings.connection: Day 1 changed one number and fixed the answer afterwards. Day 2 changes both numbers so the answer never changes.
watchFor: Both numbers moved the same way (50 + 27 for 49 + 26): ask "Did the total stay the same?"
Right amount, only one number changed (50 + 26 = 76): ask "Where did the 1 come from?"
"Add one, take one" with no reason: ask "Why does the total stay the same?" Show two jumps, one growing by 1 and one shrinking by 1.
Students who prefer Day 1's method: accept it, then ask for a second way.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: "same answer as problem 1", or moving 1 from 26 to 49. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why?" Word choice: "give 1 to 49, take 1 from 26".

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why is the total the same?
Added 1 to both. Ask: what happened to the total?

problems.notes: Look for: moving 2. Ask: "How many does 48 need? Where do they come from?"
Look for: 40 + 35. Ask: "Which number did you make friendly, and why?"

responses.tip: Moved the other way. Same total.
Ask: if you add 1 to one number, what do you do to the other?

problems.notes: Look for: 60 + 35. Ask: "What changed from problem 4? What happened to the total?"

responses.say: It's 20 more than the last one.

problems.notes: Look for: 70 + 35. Ask: "How much did you move this time?"

responses.tip: Gave 2 but didn't take 2. Ask: where did the 2 come from?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 45, or Day 1's way (198 + 50, then back 3). Ask: "Both work. Which is easier here, and why?"

responses.tip: Give and take.
Day 1's way. Ask: which is easier here?
Added 2 to both. Ask: what happened to the total?

strings.title: Subtraction as Distance
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Subtraction finds the distance between two numbers. Start at the smaller number and add up to the larger.
strings.keywords: distance, difference, gap, how far, add up.
strings.connection: The jumps from Days 1 and 2 now go from the smaller number up to the larger.
watchFor: Borrowing in their heads (21 or 12 for 100 − 89): ask "Where are 89 and 100 on the line?"
10 on problem 3: the 1 from 89 to 90 was left out. Ask "Did you start at 89 or at 90?"
24 on problem 7 (copying the pattern): ask "Are 1002 and 1000 the same number?"
Taking away instead of adding up: accept it, then ask "Which way was the shorter jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "How far is 90 from 100?"
Look for: "98 to 100 is 2" instead of taking away 98. Ask: "Is it easier to take away 98 or to see how far 98 is from 100?"

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why add up instead of take away?
Regrouping slip. Ask: is 98 close to 100? How far?

problems.notes: Look for: 89 to 90 (1), then 90 to 100 (10). Ask: "Where did you stop on the way?"

responses.tip: Regrouping slip. Ask: how far is 89 from 90? From 100?

problems.notes: Look for: 76 to 80 (4), then 80 to 100 (20), or one jump from 76 to 100. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?"

responses.tip: Regrouping slip (10 − 7 = 3). Ask: how far is 76 from 80? From 100?

problems.notes: Look for: the same gap as problem 4. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why is it the same?" Word choice: "same gap", "same distance".

responses.say: Same as 100 − 76, just 200 more on each.
responses.tip: Ask: why is the gap the same?

problems.notes: Look for: the same gap again. Ask: "Predict 5000 − 4976 before I show it."

responses.tip: Ask: is the answer closer to 24 or to 124? How far is 976 from 1000?

problems.notes: Look for: the gap from problem 6, plus 2. Ask: "What changed from problem 6? What happened to the answer?" Word choice: "the top number moved up 2, so the gap grew by 2".

responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: The top number went up 2, so the gap is 2 more.

responses.tip: Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did the gap get bigger or smaller?

strings.title: Constant Difference
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Sliding both numbers the same amount in the same direction keeps the difference the same. Slide both to make the subtraction friendlier.
strings.keywords: slide, shift, same difference, constant difference.
strings.connection: Day 2 kept the total by moving the numbers in opposite directions. Day 4 keeps the difference by moving both the same way. Day 3, problems 5 and 6 are the first hint.
watchFor: Slid only one number (62 − 50 = 12 for 62 − 49): ask "Did the gap stay the same?" Show both ends moving on the line.
Slid in opposite directions (63 − 48): that is Day 2's move. Ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
"Add 1 to both" with no reason: ask "What happens to the distance between two points if both slide the same way?"
Slid one number, then fixed the answer (62 − 50 = 12, then add 1): this works. Name it as another way.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact.
Look for: the gap is still 4. Ask: "Is this harder than 12 − 8? Why not?"

responses.tip: Ask: why is the gap the same?

problems.notes: Look for: 49 to 50 (1), then 50 to 62 (12), or sliding both up 1 to 63 − 50. Ask: "What did you do to make 49 friendlier?"

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Moved only one number. Ask: did the gap stay the same?

problems.notes: Look for: the same answer as problem 3. Ask: "What changed from problem 3? What happened to the answer? Why?" Word choice: "I slid both numbers up 1, so the difference stayed the same".

responses.say: 63 − 50 is 13, same as the last one.
responses.tip: Ask: what changed, and what didn't?

problems.notes: Look for: sliding both up 1 to 163 − 150. Ask: "Predict before I show it."
Look for: the same slide. Ask: "Does the answer depend on how big the numbers are, or how far apart they are?"

responses.tip: Ask: does size matter, or only the gap?

problems.notes: Look for: sliding both up 2 to 73 − 40, or adding up 38 to 40 to 71 (2 + 31). Ask: "Can you slide and add up? Which was quicker?"

responses.tip: Moved only one number. Ask: did the gap stay the same?

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between adding up (distance) and sliding both numbers (same difference), based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: add up, slide, friendly number, efficient, choose.
strings.connection: Combines Days 3 and 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up the slide with Day 2's opposite move: ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"

problems.notes: Look for: adding up. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?"
Look for: adding up from 48, or sliding to 54 − 50.

responses.tip: Smaller digit from the larger (8 − 2). Ask: are 52 and 48 really 16 apart?

problems.notes: Look for: 38 to 40 to 70 (2 + 30), or sliding to 72 − 40. Ask: "Which did you choose?"

responses.tip: Smaller digit from the larger. Ask: is 38 close to 40? About how far to 70?

problems.notes: Look for: sliding to 85 − 40, or adding up 39 to 40 to 84 (1 + 44).

responses.tip: Moved only one number. Ask: did the gap stay the same?

problems.notes: Look for: sliding both up 3 to 606 − 300. Ask: "What made this one easy to slide?"

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: what made it easy to slide?
Ask: is 297 close to 300? About how far is it to 603?

problems.notes: Look for: adding up 385 to 400 to 1000 (15 + 600), or sliding up 15 to 1015 − 400. Ask: "Why might adding up feel easier here?"

responses.tip: Adding up. Ask: why might this feel easier?
Regrouping slip. Ask: how far is 385 from 400? From 1000?

problems.notes: Look for: sliding both up 2 to 2402 − 2000. Ask: "Which strategy fits this one? How can you tell from the numbers?"

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Slid the wrong way. Ask: which slide makes 1998 friendly?

strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: if one number is close to a friendly number, add up or slide, and pick whichever you can do fastest.

strings.title: Times 5 as Half of Times 10
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Multiply by 10 first (easy), then halve to multiply by 5.
strings.keywords: times ten, half, five is half of ten
strings.connection: Week 1 used a friendly number and fixed the answer afterwards. Here the friendly multiplier is 10, and halving fixes it.
watchFor: Halving the wrong number first (18 x 5 as 9 x 5 = 45): ask "Is 18 x 5 about half of 18 x 10, or half of 18?"
Counting by fives or picturing the column method: ask "What would you do for 64 x 5?"
Stuck halving 170 or 340: ask "What is half of 100? Half of 70?" Then add the halves.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does halving 18 x 10 give 18 x 5?" Land: 5 is half of 10, so 5 groups is half of 10 groups.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: half of 80. Ask: "Can 8 x 10 help you with 8 x 5?" Word choice: "half of ten groups is five groups". Model: ratio 1:8, 10:80, 5:40

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why half?
Doubled instead of halving. Ask: is 5 more or less than 10?

problems.notes: Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this one too."
Look for: half of 180. Ask: "What is the same as 8 x 5?" Model: ratio 1:18, 10:180, 5:90

responses.tip: Ask: is 18 × 5 more or less than 18 × 10?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 240. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 1:24, 10:240, 5:120
Look for: half of 360. Ask: "Where does the 180 come from?" Model: ratio 1:36, 10:360, 5:180

responses.tip: Double and halve. Tomorrow's strategy.
Ask: what's 36 × 10? Then what do you do?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 170. Ask: "What did you do with the 170?" Word choice: "half of 170 is 85". Model: ratio 1:17, 10:170, 5:85

responses.tip: Ask: what is half of 170? Half of 100 and half of 70?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 640. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 1:64, 10:640, 5:320

strings.title: Double and Halve
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Halve one factor and double the other: the product stays the same and one factor becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: double, halve, same product, friendly number
strings.connection: Day 1 used x10 and halved the answer. Day 2 halves one factor and doubles the other, so the answer never changes (like Week 1, Day 2, Give and Take).
watchFor: Halved both numbers (16 x 25 as 8 x 12.5): ask "Did the product stay the same? What did you do to the 25?"
Doubled both numbers: ask "Is 32 x 50 the same size as 16 x 25?"
A move with no reason ("I just halved it"): ask "Why does the answer stay the same?" Show 4 x 25 as 4 groups of 25, regrouped as 2 groups of 50.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What did you look for in the numbers?" Land: look for a factor you can halve that turns the other factor into a friendly number (25 to 50 to 100).

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact (four quarters). Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: double 100, or 4 x 50. Ask: "What do you notice about 8 x 25 and 4 x 50?" Model: halve 8 x 25 = 4 x 50 = 2 x 100

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Doubled both. Ask: is the area the same?

problems.notes: Look for: 8 x 50, then 4 x 100. Ask: "How many times did you halve? Why stop there?" Model: halve 16 x 25 = 8 x 50 = 4 x 100
Look for: 6 x 50 = 3 x 100, or 3 x 4 x 25. Ask: "What did you do first?" Model: halve 12 x 25 = 6 x 50 = 3 x 100
Look for: 7 x 50, or 10 x 25 + 4 x 25. Ask: "Both work. Which was quicker, and why?" Model: halve 14 x 25 = 7 x 50
Look for: 9 x 100. Ask: "Which number did you halve? What did the 50 become?" Model: halve 18 x 50 = 9 x 100

responses.tip: Doubled only one. Ask: what did you do to the 18?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, or 15 x 10 + 15 x 2. Ask: "Which number would you double here, and why?" Model: halve 15 x 12 = 30 x 6

responses.tip: Ask: why double the 15?
Doubled without halving. Ask: what happens to the other factor?

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Multiply by a friendly number just over, then take back the extra groups.
strings.keywords: over, take back, groups, one less group
strings.connection: Week 1, Day 1 went over a ten and took back the extra. Here we go over to a friendly multiplier and take back whole groups.
watchFor: Took back 1, not 1 group (9 x 7 as 70 - 1 = 69): ask "How many sevens are we taking back?"
Used the wrong direction (9 x 7 as 70 + 7): ask "Is 9 x 7 more or less than 10 x 7?"
Counting by nines: accept the answer, then ask "What would you do for 99 x 5?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you take back each time?" Land: one less than a friendly number means one less group, so take back one copy of the other number.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: 70 - 7. Ask: "Can 10 x 7 help you with 9 x 7?" Word choice: "one less group". Model: array 10-1 x 7

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Took away 1, not one group. Ask: how big is each group?

problems.notes: Look for: 80 - 8. Ask: "What is the same as 9 x 7?" Model: array 10-1 x 8

responses.tip: Took away a 9. Ask: what is the size of the group you took back?

problems.notes: Look for: 70 + 7. Ask: "Over or under 10 groups? What do you add?" Model: array 10+1 x 7
Look for: 20 x 8 = 160, then - 8. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: area 20-1 x 8

responses.tip: Took back 1 instead of one group. Ask: how many 8s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, then - 6. Ask: "Predict what someone will do." Model: area 30-1 x 6
Look for: 50 x 4 = 200, then - 4. Ask: "What is the same about the last three?" Model: area 50-1 x 4
Look for: 100 x 5 = 500, then - 5. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 100-1 x 5

responses.tip: Times 5 as half of times 10. Name it.
Ask: how many 5s too many?

strings.title: Dividing by 5
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Double the dividend, then divide by 10: dividing by 5 gives the same answer as dividing double by double.
strings.keywords: double, divide by ten, same answer, how many fives
strings.connection: Day 1 halved to multiply by 5. Day 4 does the opposite: double, then divide by 10. Both use 10 as the friendly number.
watchFor: Halved instead of doubled (80 / 5 as 40 / 10 = 4): ask "Is 80 / 5 less than 80 / 10?"
Divided by 10 and stopped (80 / 5 = 8): ask "How many fives fit in 80? Is it as many as tens?"
Divided by 10 first, then doubled (135 / 10 = 13.5, then 27): accept it, name it as another way, and check the 13.5 jump.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does doubling both numbers keep the answer the same?" Land: 80 / 5 and 160 / 10 ask the same question, how many fives fit, so the answer stays the same.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: double 8, or 160 / 10. Ask: "Why is it more than 80 / 10?" Word choice: "twice as many fives as tens". Model: ratio 80:5, 160:10, 16:1

responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: There are twice as many 5s as 10s in 80: 16.

responses.tip: Halved instead of doubling. Ask: are there more 5s or more 10s in 80?

problems.notes: Look for: 70 / 10. Ask: "What did you do to 35?" Model: ratio 35:5, 70:10, 7:1
Look for: 150 / 10. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 75:5, 150:10, 15:1

responses.tip: Divided by 10 without doubling. Ask: how many 5s in 10?

problems.notes: Look for: 270 / 10. Ask: "How did you double 135?" Word choice: "double the hundred, double the thirty-five". Model: ratio 135:5, 270:10, 27:1

responses.tip: Split the dividend. Nice.

problems.notes: Look for: 480 / 10. Ask: "Is this the same move as Day 1 turned around?" Model: ratio 240:5, 480:10, 48:1
Look for: 840 / 10. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 420:5, 840:10, 84:1

responses.tip: Ask: do you double first or halve?

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between half of x10, double and halve, over and back, and double then divide by 10, based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: choose, friendly number, halve, double, over and back
strings.connection: Combines Days 1 to 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up directions (halving to divide by 5, doubling to multiply by 5): ask "Does the answer get bigger or smaller?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: look for 5, 25, 50 (halve or double), a number just under a friendly number (over and back), or a division by 5 (double).

problems.notes: Look for: half of 260. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?" Model: text 26 x 10 = 260 ; half is 130
Look for: 12 x 100, or 24 x 50 = 12 x 100. Ask: "What made 25 easy to work with?" Model: text 48 x 25 = 24 x 50 ; = 12 x 100

responses.tip: Ask: what is 4 × 25?

problems.notes: Look for: 140 - 14. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: text 10 x 14 = 140 ; 140 - 14 = 126

responses.tip: Ask: how many 14s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 390 / 10. Ask: "Which Day 4 move did you use?" Model: text 195 / 5 = 390 / 10 ; = 39
Look for: 240 - 8. Ask: "What made this one easy to adjust?" Model: text 30 x 8 = 240 ; 240 - 8 = 232
Look for: 500 - 10, or half of 980. Ask: "Two good ways. Which feels quicker, and why?" Model: text 100 x 5 = 500 ; 500 - 10 = 490

responses.tip: Ask: 2 what? How big is each group?
